extracted.intended_audience: Investigators applying for NIH grants (PIs, postdocs, research administrators)
extracted.subtask_description: Advice on post-review NIH grant administrative processes: interpreting JIT and eRA statuses, interacting with Program Officers and Grants Management Specialists, timelines for awards, decisions about resubmission or transfer, and IC-specific practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not contact GMS about award timing
rubrics_metrics.description: You should not bother the GMS, who is frantically working to catch up on a huge backlog of applications to process (therefore will not be answering PI emails) and cannot predict the award timelines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After applications are processed by the GMS, they wait in line again for approval by the IC Director before an award is issued, and the GMS will have no idea about this timeframe. Let GMS contact you if they need anything; avoid emailing them for timeline estimates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fiscal-year deadline risk for delayed regulatory approvals/JIT
rubrics_metrics.description: At the end of the FY, absolutely. Awards must be made before Oct 1, so if an applicant cannot turn around regulatory approvals in time, their application will be skipped.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Early in the FY delays due to moves or pending IACUC/IRB amendments are usually accommodated; late-FY delays risk being passed over. Keep POs informed about pending approvals.

rubrics_metrics.name: How to handle an unresponsive Program Officer (PO)
rubrics_metrics.description: If a PO is unresponsive when they should be able to convey useful information, try calling versus email, in case your correspondence is just lost; engage their Branch/Division chief (copy or contact the supervisor) with a specific, timely question.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be respectful and ask focused, time-sensitive questions (e.g., should I resubmit? how will a move affect award?). Avoid vague complaints. Escalate only for concrete issues; POs manage large portfolios and may genuinely have no new information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meaning of JIT from an IC (versus generic OER JIT)
rubrics_metrics.description: A JIT request from an IC (e.g., NIMHD) is much more promising than the generic one that the NIH Office of Extramural Research sends to every application with a score above 40.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: IC-specific JIT means they are going to do an administrative review in preparation for a possible award; it is not guaranteed but indicates serious consideration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasons an application can be skipped during administrative review
rubrics_metrics.description: Various award types might uncover reasons to skip or change the award during the administrative review, such as duplicate funding for the same work, the PI status change (move, health/family issues), or mentor/advisor withdrawal for Ks and Fs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are expected contingencies (not hidden gotchas). For career awards, acceptance of a faculty position can disqualify K99 recipients per NIH policy. PIs should anticipate and report such changes promptly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Payline and programmatic priority handling
rubrics_metrics.description: ICs may use percentiles or impact-score thresholds, but for certain FOAs (e.g., RFAs or COVID-related FOAs) percentiles may not apply and ICs may rank by score and apply programmatic priorities rather than strict rank order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An RFA may not fund strictly by rank; programmatic fit and priority can change funding decisions. For some priority areas (e.g., ADRD PAs) separate thresholds may apply.

rubrics_metrics.name: Council vs IC Director roles in funding decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Council reviews the quality of peer review and approves a paylist of applications for the IC Director to consider for funding, but IC Directors make all final funding decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Council approval does not guarantee an award; the paylist typically contains more applications than can be funded to provide backups.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expect long and variable administrative review timelines
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'Pending administrative review' status can last for months; a lengthy 'pending' period does not mean extra scrutiny.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Backlogs (e.g., Cycle 1 processing) and appropriations timing slow processing. Awards made since Oct 1 may be for emergency funding; regular applications can take many months from review to NoA.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cycle- and IC-specific timing expectations
rubrics_metrics.description: Funding and processing timelines vary by review cycle and by IC (e.g., some ICs process K99 awards later in the fiscal year and NIAID may not make K99 awards until July–September).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware of IC-specific SOPs (e.g., NIAID waits to see entire pool before committing) and requested start dates can influence perceived timing; check with PO or admin for IC norms.

rubrics_metrics.name: When to prepare and submit a resubmission (A1)
rubrics_metrics.description: If you have not received a JIT request or seen any change in eRA status by the deadline for resubmission, be prepared to submit an A1; if your PO recommends resubmission, follow their guidance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Get a revised application ready in case your A0 is not awarded; you can always withdraw an A1 if the A0 later receives an award. Ask the PO whether to resubmit and whether the FOA will be renewed.

rubrics_metrics.name: How to interpret status changes like 'Award prepared'
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Award prepared: refer questions to Grants Management Specialist' often means the award is waiting for the IC Director to sign off and a NoA may be imminent (e.g., tomorrow or next week).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Status progression varies by IC; 'award prepared' is farther along than 'pending administrative review' and often precedes the NoA.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling application transfer to a new institution
rubrics_metrics.description: Your university should be willing to transfer the application, but the NIH needs to approve your new institution as capable (appropriate facilities, resources, & personnel) of conducting the reviewed research.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inform the PO as soon as possible so they can confirm transfer feasibility. Budgeted work retained by prior institution is a negotiation between institutions; NIH does not decide transfer terms. Alternatively, withdraw and resubmit from the new institution to avoid entanglement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Approach to PO communications about urgent questions before Council
rubrics_metrics.description: POs (or directors) may request urgent clarifications before Council because Council evaluates peer review quality and appropriateness for the IC mission; clarification may be requested if something concerned reviewers or Council members.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Respond promptly to such requests; they can influence Council deliberations and funding consideration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Study section scoring disparities have limited remediation
rubrics_metrics.description: Being reviewed in a study section that scores more harshly may make a slight difference if you are just over the payline, but you would not receive special consideration simply because your panel is 'tough'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a PO is unresponsive about this, escalate to career development contacts or division leadership with focused questions; don't expect scoring normalization in your favor solely due to panel differences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don’t over-interpret long delays as negative signals
rubrics_metrics.description: Delays in processing or long 'pending' statuses are often due to backlog, staffing, or prioritization (e.g., COVID applications) rather than heightened scrutiny or a problem with the application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sit tight unless you are contacted for additional documents; check with PO only after a reasonable wait (and use escalation channels for timely, specific needs).
